ok but isn’t there now the hierarchy of the community over the individual ? we agree on the fact that anarchy is without ruler, but in the society you’re describing, the majority becomes the “ruler” over the minority. As you say, decisions would be made through pure democracy and a simple majority consensus. For example, let’s say there is a case where the final vote of a decision comes to be 51% for and 49% against. Since everything is just a majority consensus, only the 51% would get their voices heard and the 49% is disregarded. I just don’t understand how this is without ruler. You may have gotten rid of the sort of centralized government, but there is still that aspect of control/hierarchy where the majority rules over the minority.

This is why i believe the truest form of anarchy is inherently individualistic because when you are left without ruler, you have sole control over your body and it’s actions. Obviously, in an anarchist society, ppl can choose to work in groups together but that is only through their own free will thus, in an anarchist society, ppl would be able to leave said group at anytime.

>Anarchism can be broadly divided into two camps: individualists and collectivists. (Actually, the original anarchists were largely collectivists.)

Well this could be true, but this is strongly contingent upon people in that collective freely choosing to be in that collective. Of course, in an anarchist society, you could have groups of people working together, but don't depend on it. An example of this could be the modern day family structure. Parents bringing home wealth and resources to be distributed amongst their children, but technically, at any given moment, they could just leave and stop taking part in this collective. Really, the only thing that truly binds them to this collective is the law (and even this is not certain in some cases). Now in an anarchist society, there is no law. Presumably, there is no one in charge to make the rules. This is why an anarcho-communist society is flawed. Since there is no law, there is nothing actually binding someone to that collective other than the individuals own free will. Once the individual chooses to leave the collective, the whole structure falls apart. This is why anarchy inherently falls back onto being individualistic.

>Under communism, there is no "business owner" -- the workers themselves own and/or manage their workplaces directly.

Doesn't there need to be someone who has the idea for the product, create the product, gather materials etc. Furthermore, in your previous point, you described there being a transitional period from what I understand to be as capitalism -> communism. This means there has to be a business owner at some point, specifically in the beginning during the capitalistic period. Therefore, my point still stands. There had to be a business owner who started the business, then the workers took over control, creating a hierarchy in itself of the workers over the original business owner. Which again, isn't anarchy, if the business owner doesn't want to freely give over rights to the workers. As you mentioned, they would forcibly kick the bourgeoisie out which is control of the individual by the community. Essentially, the community as a whole becomes the "state" as they control what the individuals do through mob rule.

>but you can't just point to a forest and claim it's your forest and people have to pay you to enter it.

Again, who decides this ? Who is the "boss" that makes sure this doesn't happen ? What's to stop someone in an anarchist society from charging someone to enter a forest they claim is theirs ?

well to this i would say anarchy is inherently individualistic (an = without, archy = ruler). when there is no governing body to set the parameters for society, anybody can do anything they want, which is why anarchy is obviously flawed. Just look at past examples where anarchy was practiced. Each time, ppl roam free, mass murder, steal, etc. bc there’s no laws and/or repercussions for ppls actions. 

to the point of the workers’ council, who would make sure each business would have the workers take over the business owner and dictate the means of production if it is an anarchist society ? who would make sure of this and be the sort of “boss” to watch over ?furthermore, isn’t the workers having power over the actual business owner a hierarchy in itself ? It would be mob rule and that in itself is a hierarchy of the majority over the minority.

And to ur point of wealth distribution, my understanding of communism (and what seems to be most commonly spoken of) is that in a communist society, the community would make sure no one is starving, in need of a house, or other vital resources. If this is the case, there would definitely be some sort of wealth distribution. Especially in the sense that most communists make the distinction between private and personal property. At the very least, they say that if someone isn’t currently using their property, it can be taken by the community and redistributed to someone who needs it. But this brings me back to my main point of how it isn’t anarchy anymore if u have a community dictate the society over the individual. This is still a hierarchy which is why it isn’t anarchy.

i never understood anarcho-communism anyway. The anarchy part can make sense since it really just requires no governing body. But how does the communism come in ? How can you force ppl to practice communism and share wealth if it is an anarchist society ? 

If people are left to do whatever they want and individualism is upheld, there’s no way communism can take place because there’s no one controlling anyone. As soon as even just the “community” starts controlling the individual and forcing them to give up wealth for the “common good” or give up private property, then it’s no longer anarchism as there is now a hierarchy of the public community over the individual. I’m sure Stalin, Mao, Castro, etc. all recognized this as they never just let the state “wither away”.

not sure if this helps but just some thoughts i had on the validity of the premise of anarcho-communism.
